answer: Before 1948 most Jewish-held land was bought: of 1,731,300 dunams at the end of 1944, the Survey of Palestine counts 1,556,700 as purchased and 174,600 as government concessions, 6.6 percent of Palestine's area; other counts run from about 1.49 to 2 million dunams. That share is of the whole country, nearly half of it desert on the Survey's figures. Most purchases were from large, often absentee, landowners, and the Jewish National Fund held its land as the inalienable property of the Jewish people. But sales displaced Arab tenants: Hope Simpson (1930) concluded that of 688 tenant families on Jezreel-valley land Jews had bought, 309 had joined the landless, and area officers counted 1,270 farmers displaced. He also wrote that the Jewish authorities had 'nothing with which to reproach themselves' there; the duty to protect tenants lay with the government. In 1940 Britain restricted sales.

facts.text: The Survey of Palestine says Jewish-owned land was 1,731,300 dunams at the end of 1944, of which 1,556,700 were purchased and 174,600 were government concessions, 6.6 percent of Palestine's area. Other counts differ by source, date and definition, so they are not a trend: about 1,588,000 dunams registered in Jewish names at the end of 1945 (also the Survey, which assumes 650,000 dunams were owned before 1920 and excludes land held by Jews as tenants but not registered); 1,514,247 dunams on 1 April 1943 (Survey, vol. II); 1,491,699 dunams on 1 April 1945 (Village Statistics, as quoted by a UN study; it is lower than the Survey's 1943 figure for reasons the sources do not give); and about 2 million dunams by May 1948 (Stein's estimate: his text calls it purchased, his table heads it 'total land accumulated to date from all sources'). The 6.6 percent is a share of the whole land area, including desert and state land; it is not a share of farmland or of privately owned land.

facts.text: The Survey of Palestine gives Palestine's total land area as about 26,320 square kilometres, of which about 12,077 lie in the 'deserts of Beersheba' (the Negev), about 46 percent. The Survey is inconsistent with itself by about 500 square kilometres: elsewhere it gives 13,743 for the rest, which sums to 25,820. The Survey adds that there may be private claims to over 2,000 square kilometres of that desert, cultivated from time to time. The UN committee called the Negev south of latitude 31 desert land of little agricultural value, and Stein notes the land Jews bought was not south of Beersheba. So the 6.6 percent is a share of a country of which, on the Survey's figures, nearly half is desert.

facts.text: The Survey of Palestine's ownership table lumps 'Arabs and other non-Jews' together, so government (state, municipal) land is in that column. In the settled areas the Survey found over 660 square kilometres of public land (of nearly 4,500 whose ownership had been settled), with about 900 more probably government property; it gives state domain as 616,000 dunums settled and 927,000 claimed (a different count and date). These figures do not add up to a share of the whole country, and no source on this card gives one; much of the desert was never settled for title. Hope Simpson found in 1930 that only small areas of government land were available for settlement until developed.

facts.text: Smaller and resident owners also sold, and many sellers were in debt. Stein finds Arab offers to sell came from large and small landowners alike, but that purchases were mostly of large holdings from relatively few owners; he writes that for most Arabs their sagging economic condition forced them to sell, and reports that the JNF buyer Yehoshua Hankin told Hope Simpson in 1930 that 90 percent of the sellers were in debt (a buyer's statement). Hope Simpson, quoting the Director of Education, records that hardly any Arab village exists which is not in debt. The Peel Commission's summary says many Arab landowners benefited from the sale of land.

facts.text: Britain created an official register of 'landless Arabs' in 1931 (Lewis French, Director of Development); by 1 January 1936 it had admitted 664 of 3,271 applicants and disallowed 2,607. facts.text: Displaced farmers and their communities protested in their own terms. A scholarly study of the Sursuq (Sursock) family's accounts says peasants of Jidru wrote frequent petitions to local officials complaining that the companies were stealing their product, and earlier tenants held back a harvest and petitioned the German consul and Ottoman officials. In 1933 seven Bedouin sheikhs removed from the Wadi Hawarith lands applied to the president of the Nablus district court to set aside the order for their removal (JTA news report). Hope Simpson in 1930 reports that everywhere there is the complaint that many cultivators have lost their land.

contested.text: How much of the displacement purchases caused is disputed. Hope Simpson (1930) concluded, from the Jewish Agency's own list, that 309 of 688 tenant families on the Esdraelon villages had joined the landless, and reported the area officers' count of 1,270 farmers displaced; the Agency's memorandum, which he quotes, said very few of those traced were landless. Stein, in one passage, gives three cases: on the 200,000 dunams of Sursock land fewer than 700 Arab tenants worked, perhaps 5,000 people in all; at Shatta (14,000 dunams, bought 1929-30) there were 900 Arabs; at Wadi Hawarith and Wadi Qabbani (30,000 dunams, bought 1929-30) there were 1,200 Bedouin families. In its official 1937 summary the Peel Commission judged that the shortage of land was due less to purchase by Jews than to the increase in the Arab population, while urging care for tenants. The 1936 register of landless Arabs admitted 664 applicants under a strict definition.

could_not_verify: The shares bought from absentee owners, from resident large owners and from small farmers: I found only Stein's 'more than 60 percent from absentee landlords in the 1920s' and his rejection of the 9.4 percent peasant figure. The Granott breakdown (52.6, 24.6, 13.4 and 9.4 percent) and Porath's work are not on any readable page I found, so they are not quoted.
Lewis French's report itself (1931-32) was not found; his work is described through the Survey of Palestine, which counts the registered landless at 664.

Figures for Jewish-owned land differ (1.49, 1.51, 1.59, 1.73 and 2.0 million dunams): the card says which source gives which, but I could not tell from the pages whether Stein's 2 million is purchases or holdings, or whether Jewish totals before 1920 (650,000 assumed) are firm.
The Survey of Palestine is cited from the Berman Jewish Policy Archive's scan of a 1946 British government publication; I found no archive.org copy readable here.
Reviewer: Hope Simpson also criticised JNF lease terms (no Arab labour); that is in the cited report but not carried as a fact.

A single state-land share for the whole country: the Survey gives public land only for the settled areas (over 660 square kilometres of nearly 4,500 settled) and state domain in dunums (616,000 settled, 927,000 claimed), and its ownership table lumps all non-Jews. A person would need the Survey's land-settlement tables (vol. I, chapter on land) read with the Village Statistics 1945 land-ownership volume, and a scholar who has reconciled them.
The Survey's Negev figures are inconsistent by about 500 square kilometres (12,077 + 13,743 is not 26,320); I could not find a second source for the Negev area.

The Shaw Commission's report is quoted from the Institute for Palestine Studies' reproduction of its summary of findings and from the Center for Online Judaic Studies' page-cited excerpts; I did not find a library scan of the full Cmd. 3530.

Displaced farmers in their own words after 1922: the Wadi Hawarith tenants' article by Raya Adler (International Journal of Middle East Studies, 1988) and Middle Eastern Studies 52 (2016), 135-152, would quote petitions and testimony; neither page was readable here. The card's displaced-side fact rests on a 2024-era IJMES article (mostly pre-1922 and wartime), one 1933 news item and Hope Simpson's report of complaints.

Facts 1, 2, 3, 7 and 9 do not meet the record rule's two confirming reliable sources, or rest on Stein alone; what a person would need is a second scholar on JNF holdings (for example Alexander Kedar or Fredrik Meiton) and a library copy of the Village Statistics land-ownership volume.

Fact 4 (Article 6) and fact 11's White Paper are the Mandate and White Paper texts themselves; the UN committee report and the Survey reproduce the Mandate text, so they confirm our reading, not the Mandate's effect.
not_claimed: This card does not say the land was 'empty' or that all sellers were willing; Hope Simpson and the Peel report document displacement and its limits.
It does not say purchases were illegal; they were legal under the Mandate, and restricted from 1940.
It does not cover the land that changed hands in and after 1948.
It does not say 6.6 percent is the share of cultivable land; the Survey's own table shows Jewish ownership of cultivable categories was larger.

answer_claims.says: Before 1948 most Jewish-held land was bought: of 1,731,300 dunams at the end of 1944, the Survey of Palestine counts 1,556,700 as purchased and 174,600 as government concessions, 6.6 percent of Palestine's area; other counts run from about 1.49 to 2 million dunams.
That share is of the whole country, nearly half of it desert on the Survey's figures.
Most purchases were from large, often absentee, landowners, and the Jewish National Fund held its land as the inalienable property of the Jewish people.

But sales displaced Arab tenants: Hope Simpson (1930) concluded that of 688 tenant families on Jezreel-valley land Jews had bought, 309 had joined the landless, and area officers counted 1,270 farmers displaced.
He also wrote that the Jewish authorities had 'nothing with which to reproach themselves' there; the duty to protect tenants lay with the government.

skeptic.notes: Read 2+ sources for every fact (12) in context, including both volumes of the Survey. Figures check out against the Survey. Five Jewish-owned totals: all five are on their pages; they differ by date and definition (concessions, registered vs held, assumption of 650,000 before 1920, Stein's 'all sources'); the 1,491,699 for April 1945 is lower than the 1,514,247 for April 1943 and the sources do not say why; the fact now says so and says they are not a trend. 6.6 percent is the Survey's share of total land area (1,731,300 of 26,320 km2); the fact now says it is not of farmland or private land. [must-fix] Old answer began 'Jews bought land; they did not seize it' but 174,600 dunams (10 percent of the 1944 total) were government concessions, and the UN study on the card says the rest not bought came by Mandatory cessions or from religious charities; reworded to 'most ... was bought'. [must-fix] Contested[0] said 'both agree tenants were displaced; they differ on blame' with no quote from Khalidi or Stein saying so; removed. Added a blame entry from Hope Simpson (the Jewish authorities 'have nothing with which to reproach themselves'; the duty was the government's), which the card omitted and which the Israeli side would cite. [must-fix] Palestinian side: Stein's 'fewer than 700 tenants, perhaps 5,000 people' (Sursock) was quoted while the same passage records 900 Arabs on 14,000 dunams (Shatta) and 1,200 Bedouin families on 30,000 dunams (Wadi Hawarith); added. Hope Simpson's 309 of 688 is his reading of the Jewish Agency's own list, which said 'very few' were landless; both now shown. [must-fix] Fact 10 (Shaw) rests on three summaries, none of which is the report; now said in the text, with the report's stated primary cause (political and national aspirations) alongside the economic fear. [should-fix] Fact 2 (state land): the two Survey volumes and a PLO-reprint (advocacy) are one origin; 660 km2 and 616,000 dunums are different counts; no whole-country state-land figure exists on the card. Fact 6: the 90 percent debt figure is JNF buyer Hankin's claim to Hope Simpson, not Stein's finding; fixed. Fact 11: 'got around them' rests on Stein alone; said. Fact 1: Survey internal inconsistency (12,077 + 13,743 = 25,820, not 26,320) and the Survey's 2,000 km2 of possible private claims in the Negev are now on the card. Stein's 2 million: 'purchased' in text, 'from all sources' in his table. [should-fix] Missing: JNF lease terms (Hope Simpson), the Peel finding that tenants were displaced, and any Bedouin-side source. Stein supplies five facts and three of the contested entries: one scholar. 'heard' (Khalidi on the Jewish Colonization Agency) is a weak form of the claim; the stronger one, 1948, is deferred to another card. Strongest objections: Palestinian side, tenant displacement and Bedouin claims thinly sourced; Israeli side, concessions and Hope Simpson's 'nothing to reproach' were missing.

citer.notes: 6 answer sentences, each tied to facts. Removed/reworded: 'they did not seize it' (no fact says nothing was seized; concessions are in fact 0); 'roughly 6 to 7 percent' (the Survey says 6.6; the 2 million estimate is 7.6 percent of 26.3 million, outside the range) replaced by the Survey's own 6.6 and 'other counts run from 1.49 to 2 million'; 'sales cost Arab tenant farmers their holdings' now rests on the Esdraelon evidence stated; 'Historians dispute how many were displaced and who was to blame' removed from the answer (only contested carries it); 'state land is part of the rest' reworded (the Negev is largely state or unsettled land too). The cultivable-land fact (3) is not used by the answer; should-fix: say that Jewish share of citrus land was about half and of taxable cereal land about 13 percent, so 6.6 percent is not the share of farmland.
